subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If n is a positive integer, show that (1 + i)²ⁿ + (1 − i)²ⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/2).

mark_split.label: Raise to 2n by De Moivre's theorem

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how you write 1 + i, what De Moivre's theorem does to it, and how the two powers combine.
insider_note: The mark most often lost is the first one: writing r = √2 and θ = π/4 with the quadrant checked. The rest is one theorem and one addition.

steps.label: Mod-amp form of 1 + i
steps.margin_note: First and second marks. For 1 + i: r = √(1 + 1) = √2 and tan θ = 1, so θ = π/4, with x and y both positive. The √2 outside the bracket is what produces the power of 2 in the answer.
steps.memory_tip: r = √(1 + 1) = √2 and θ = π/4, both x and y positive. r is not 1 — it is what makes the power of 2.
lines: Let 1 + i = x + iy ⇒ x = 1, y = 1

recall.must_convey: That 1 + i is first written in modulus-amplitude form: r = √2 and θ = π/4, giving r(cos θ + i sin θ).
accept: first write 1 + i in mod amp form with r equal to √2 and theta equal to π/4
find the modulus and the amplitude of 1 + i and write it as r cos theta plus i sin theta
convert 1 + i to polar form r cis theta before raising the power
1 + i ni mod amp form lo rasi r √2 theta π/4 teeskovali
modulus amplitude form first, r is √2 and the angle is π/4

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem works only on a number written as cos θ + i sin θ. Pulling out r first is what makes the theorem usable, so this line is the method, not a preliminary.
common_mistakes: Writing r = 1 by habit; here r is not 1, and it is what produces the power of 2 in the answer.
Taking θ from tan θ without checking the quadrant: both x and y are positive, so θ is in the first quadrant.
Forgetting the r outside the bracket when the form is written.

steps.label: Raise to 2n by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. The power 2n goes on both parts: (√2)²ⁿ = 2ⁿ, and the angle becomes 2n · π/4 = nπ/2. Raise the modulus as an ordinary real number and multiply the angle by the same power.
steps.memory_tip: The power 2n goes on both parts: (√2)²ⁿ = 2ⁿ, and 2n · π/4 = nπ/2.

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem is applied: raising the mod-amp form to the power 2n multiplies the angle by 2n and gives 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/2) + i sin(nπ/2)), called equation (1).
accept: apply De Moivre's theorem so the angle is multiplied by 2n and we get 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/2) + i sin(nπ/2))
raise the mod amp form to the power and multiply the angle by 2n by De Moivre
by De Moivre cos theta plus i sin theta to the power gives cos n theta plus i sin n theta
De Moivre theorem apply chesi angle ni 2n tho multiply cheyyali
the power goes onto the angle by De Moivre's theorem, that is equation one

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem says (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n: the power moves onto the angle. The real factor r is raised separately, as an ordinary real number.
common_mistakes: Raising r to the power but forgetting to multiply the angle by the same power.
Multiplying the angle by the power but leaving r un-raised.
Writing (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cosⁿ θ + i sinⁿ θ, which is false.

steps.label: The conjugate power
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. 1 − i is the conjugate of 1 + i, so raising it to 2n gives the same 2ⁿ with the sine sign reversed. Label it (2); nothing is recomputed.
steps.memory_tip: 1 − i is the conjugate of 1 + i, so the same 2ⁿ with the sine sign reversed.

recall.must_convey: That the conjugate number is treated in the same way and gives 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/2) − i sin(nπ/2)), called equation (2), with the sign of the sine term changed.
accept: similarly the conjugate gives the same thing with minus i sin, that is equation two
do the same for the conjugate and only the sign of the sine changes
the second bracket is the conjugate so its power is 2ⁿ(cos(nπ/2) − i sin(nπ/2))
conjugate ki same step, sin term sign matrame minus avuthundi
equation two is the conjugate with cos minus i sin

steps.why: The second number is the conjugate of the first, so it has the same r and the angle −θ. Nothing new has to be computed; only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Recomputing r and θ from scratch and losing time.
Writing equation (2) without the minus sign, so nothing cancels in the next step.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Adding (1) and (2) cancels the i sin terms and doubles the cosine: 2ⁿ · 2 cos(nπ/2). Combine the powers of 2 into 2ⁿ⁺¹.
steps.memory_tip: Adding cancels the sines and doubles the cosine: 2ⁿ · 2 = 2ⁿ⁺¹.

recall.must_convey: That equations (1) and (2) are added, the i sin terms cancel, and the result is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/2).
accept: add one and two, the i sin terms cancel and we get 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/2)
adding the two equations the sine parts cancel leaving two times the cosine
one plus two gives two cos and the final answer is 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/2)
rendu equations add cheste sin terms cancel ayyi 2ⁿ⁺¹ cos(nπ/2) vasthundi
the imaginary parts cancel on adding and the answer is two to the n plus one times cos

steps.why: The two numbers are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part. Adding removes the i sin terms and leaves exactly the cosine the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Subtracting instead of adding, which leaves 2i sin instead of 2 cos.
Leaving the answer as 2ⁿ · 2 cos instead of combining into one power of 2.
Dropping the factor that comes from r, which is the whole reason the answer has a power of 2.
